narrative: Markets staged a modest relief bounce on Friday following a historic tech selloff, though the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 still logged their worst weekly performances since June. A resilient labor market was underscored by nonfarm payrolls surging 165k against a 70k estimate, reinforcing a higher-for-longer interest rate path. Investors are re-evaluating the AI trade amid growing scrutiny over capital discipline, infrastructure capex, and post-midterm regulatory headwinds for data centers. Meanwhile, crude oil suffered severe downward pressure, with Brent marking its worst weekly drop since April 2020. Although Q3 corporate earnings growth remains robust above 30%, persistent inflation keeps Federal Reserve easing paths uncertain ahead of upcoming price prints.

Nasdaq.why: Anchors reported a roughly 1% Friday rebound, but the index finished down 5% on the week amid severe AI valuation re-pricing and capex concerns.

S&P 500.why: Anchors noted a modest 0.31% daily gain, but the index had its worst week since June despite Q3 earnings growth tracking above 30%.

Gold.why: Gold was not covered in the provided notes.

Oil.why: Anchors reported Brent crude plunging 14% on the week, recording its sharpest decline since April 2020.

priced_in: A higher-for-longer interest rate path and a more measured pace of Fed adjustments.
Congressional gridlock in Washington following the midterm elections.
Heightened caution regarding the near-term sustainability and capital intensity of the AI trade.
Potential rebound signals stemming from extreme readings on the Goldman Sachs Market Panic Gauge.
debates: AI infrastructure build-out pacing and capital discipline pressures on hyper-scalers versus ongoing capital appetite for foundational AI models, evidenced by OpenAI's $1.25 trillion valuation.
Resilient corporate earnings growth (>30%) versus consumer spending strength being partly masked and driven by persistent inflation.
